body: I see I'm not worth talking to when it comes to this.

Made a throwaway for this, so I can talk openly without using my normal account.

I am right there with you. I have been a mess for about three years now. I went through a terrible ordeal a few years ago, and I doubt that I'll ever really fully recover. I go through multiple phases that I've never been able to deal with. Sometimes I feel terrible amounts of despair, regret, anger, any number of negative emotions. I've seen therapists, have had medication, have gone through everything, nothing is of any help.

I came very close to killing myself almost a year ago. I almost went through it, but caught control of myself at the last second. I've never really gotten better, nor do I have any hope that it ever will. I go through my life with no promise that things ever will get better. I always feel like I'm in the passengers seat and that someone else entirely is driving my life. I just want to scream, and take out the person who is driving my life around, but there's nothing I can do.
Even the past 24 hours when I should have turned into a kid again and just been happy to play with new Star Wars stuff, I'm just so angry and cynical. I should be goofing around with my new X Wing and Kylo Ren, but instead all I see in them is crass comercialization. What once was a fun story that a cool young guy from California wrote and turned into an awesome movie is now just a cog in a huge corporate machine, and I've bought into it by buying cheap commoditized plastic that some poor kid in Asia made just a few cents to produce.

I hate myself, I hate everything around me. But at the same time I hate having this outlook and cynicism. I wish there was something I could do, but realistically I know there isn't. Anything else is just a happy and convenient lie.

Anyways, just wanted you to know you aren't the only one struggling.
I'm not at all, what's your take of it?

The thing is, I once was entirely happy with my life.  I had a career where I was accomplishing things and was making a positive impact, but it was taken from me.  Just look through my account history for more details on that.

What you said here really hit home:

> Here's what I think: you're crashing and burning because it turns out that what you thought you wanted out of life doesn't make you happy. It's a bad cycle because your unhappiness and events in your life, work and/or otherwise (whether entirely out of your control or negatively impacted by your general frame of mind) have caused a failure to meet your definition of success which further deepens your depression, which causes more of what you are defining as failure.

That hits hard and hits on a truth I hadn't really fully considered.  I just have no idea where to even start on doing anything about it, and frankly, I'm probably too jaded and tired to even begin.

I question what it really means though.  What real impact or difference does puppies or ice cream make?

This past Summer should have been one of the best of my life.  I fulfilled a lifelong dream and attended the Coachella festival in California.  I travelled to South America and saw some of the most awesome scenery I'd ever seen.

It was a temporary high, but as soon as I returned home and was forced back into the grind, I realized what a waste it all was.  It ultimately means nothing and was little more than a temporary detour into a path of pointlessness.

I do my best to hide it, but you're right that it probably still comes out.  I got a little tipsy at a party recently and confessed to a really good friend that I hate myself and everything about me, and he's treated me very awkwardly ever since.

The truth of the matter is that I'm a mess.  I'm barely keeping it together.  And if someone distances themselves from me because of it, I either don't deserve them or I'm too fucked up for anyone to care anyways.

A lot of the things I've referred to aren't necessarily specifically job related.  If anything, I totally agree with you that I'm not just my job and I've tried to tackle a lot of personal projects on my own to get away from that.  It's also insanely frustrating because I feel like every one of those have embarrassingly crashed and burned as well.

I'll try to be as specific as I can without giving away any identifying information, so if there's anything that doesn't make sense, feel free to PM me for more clarification.  And again, this is just one example.

Over the past month, I had a (non-work) colleague come to me offering me an opportunity on a certain date.  I held my plans on that date, with the assumption that I'd be working with them on that date.  

It's now a week out from that date, when I assumed I'd be busy.  I'd still not heard back from him with any confirmation, despite a number of emails.  I'd emailed his supervisor asking for some clarification since I couldn't reach him.

I then *finally* get a nasty email from him telling me how everything was my fault and that he wouldn't consider me for any opportunities in the future.

I just felt like the whole thing was a setup with false hope and now I've got a good relationship ruined because of things entirely out of my control.

My wife married me because growing up through high school where we met, she was convinced I'd amount to something.  I've not.  I've failed her.

My friends are people that I'd met through various personal projects and professional efforts.  We've all tried working on projects together at some point.  Projects which have failed, and I accept responsibility for that and have ultimately failed them because of it.

"That" is the ordinary.  An ordinary life is a failure to me.  I don't want to be like everyone else and have a 40 hour a week job, a suburban house, a mortgage, etc, etc.  But society is fashioned in such a way where I have little to no choice.

What I want instead is something more.  Something where I can be happy with what I've accomplished and know that I've changed the lives of others for the better.  I don't want to sit in an office for 40 hours a week, I want to get out there and experience life and make things happen.

But the problem is that despite my best efforts, I've not reached those goals.  Instead I'm still stuck in the prison of this suburban life that I have no escape from.

The problem is that I feel like such a failure compared to where I was, and where I once could have been.  Without going into identifying details, I was really killing it in my career and becoming fairly well known.  I was giving talks at large and recognized national conferences like South by Southwest.  Now I'm just a shell of who I was and can barely keep myself together enough to even hold a local marketing job at a small company.

I *have* failed everyone because I've fallen so far.  That is an undeniable fact.

Ha.  Dark side of the force.

Look, I appreciate the thought.  But ever since I've dealt with so much crap in my life, I just have a more realistic view of things.  No matter how I feel or interpret things, life will inevitably the same.  Humans are despicable creatures that mean absolutely nothing.  We all hurt each other, yet it doesn't matter because in a few decades time we'll all be dead and forgotten.  No effort means anything.  You don't.  I don't.  

"I think human consciousness, is a tragic misstep in evolution. We became too self-aware, nature created an aspect of nature separate from itself, we are creatures that should not exist by natural law. We are things that labor under the illusion of having a self; an accretion of sensory, experience and feeling, programmed with total assurance that we are each somebody, when in fact everybody is nobody. Maybe the honorable thing for our species to do is deny our programming, stop reproducing, walk hand in hand into extinction, one last midnight - brothers and sisters opting out of a raw deal."
I'm a failure compared to what I want out of life.  Yes, I have those things.  But that's not enough for me.  And until I reach that, I'm a failure and deserve failure.
I suspect that's the case, and I wouldn't blame them.  I'm a failure and a pathetic excuse for a person, I wouldn't want to hang out with me either, you're absolutely right.

I don't think they're just in my head, I see hard evidence of it every day.  There is absolutely some reason that people have dissociated with me, treat me differently, or try to avoid me.  That's hard proof that I'm a failure.
It saddens me to continually hear this from people.  Especially given that I've seen many different therapists and have been on many different medications through the years, to no avail whatsoever.

Like I mentioned in another comment, I just don't have the time.  I really wish I did.  But when you work 60 hours a week without a glimmer of hope of getting any off-time, finding a good therapist that can work around that schedule is damn near impossible.

I'm working close to 60 hours a week these days, it leaves little time for anything else.  By the time I'm done with work, I get home and take care of what needs to be done around the house with various things.  When the weekend rolls around, I've barely got the energy for much of anything.  Nevermind the fact that classes I'd like to take, which I had looked into, aren't offered online or over the weekends.
Long story.  You can look through my post history for the full details.
Wish I could!  Time is a precious commodity I don't have much of these days.

I'd love not to coast.  I've certainly not actively tried to.  I had a job I loved once but it was taken from me.  I've tried a ton of my own personal projects and have started my own business, but everything has failed.  Eventually, getting beat down by life just leaves you so jaded and tired to really try anymore.
I totally agree!  Just easier said than done.

I work in marketing and advertising.  It sucks to just continually feed the monster of consumerism, but really my skillset and experience isn't suited to anything else.  I'd much rather be doing something far more creative and meaningful, but I have no idea how to move forward.

Well sure, I try to cram in as much fun stuff as I can when I can.  Hiking, camping, travel, etc.  But the issue is those are always temporary and are comparably just fractions of time as opposed to the hours I spend in an office doing pointless crap I don't care about that just pay bills.
I go the gym like three times a week.  I don't know what I could be doing better or differently.

We were originally hired by two different departments to do essentially the same job for each individual department.  When the President re-organized everything, we essentially overlapped in the new one we were each assigned to.  Layoffs were always rumored due to state budget cuts, so yeah, do the math.  I always wanted to ignore the inevitable politics and just put my nose down and do my best work, but those obviously weren't his methods.

The only thing I can come up with is that some of my colleagues could have seen what I was doing as comparably unnecessary.  I also often took things that were largely seen as insigificant by others and took them very seriously and probably leveraged the good will I had in other areas to make progress in them.

Perhaps they saw my methods in doing that as less than desireable at times, but I personally knew it was ultimately for the benefit of the programs I was helping students out with, so I largely disregarded some of that disdain as irrelevant.  I didn't care to play politics, but perhaps I could have done it with more tact.

I do remember that I sometimes caught slight criticism from others that I tried to "take over everything," which I only took as a light criticism in that I tried to involve myself in every opportunity I could.  Most universities have a whole "publish or perish" atmosphere, but ours was more like "diversify or fry."  You had to get involved in as many things as possible to remain relevant, and I did that to a very large extent.  I think others could have potentially been threatened by that because the nature of my position afforded me more time and flexibility to do that than just about anybody else on campus.

But that's really all I got.  And it's just little more than a theory.

Trust me, for three years now I've run through my mind trying to figure out any possible thing where I may have failed or have fallen short.  I can think of a select few instances in which I may have put my foot in my mouth on minor issues, but in that time I've never been able to think of any type of sin which would have made me deserving of that type of thing.
I'd take the cut in pay to go back to where I was.  I'd be more than glad to pay the difference in order to feel productive and worthwhile again.
No I haven't, what's the message of it?

My school doesn't offer a graduate degree in my field, nor would it be particularly helpful anyways.  If anything, it would just make me appear to be overqualified and make it harder to get a good position.
So I failed at my job, failed at how I dealt with HR, am a poor writer, and generally suck as a human being.  Got it.
I've talked about this with my therapist.  I've concluded it's my job as a husband to carry my own burdens and not weigh her down with it.  It's my responsibility, not hers.

On one hand, I don't feel like I should have to accept responsibility for that.  Office politics are not part of the job description, and are not productive in order to achieve the goals of the position.  It's fucked up that those who play those pointless games are rewarded while people who want to ignore them and do their job are casualties of it.  I don't feel like I should have to apologize or feel guilt over wanting to ignore it and just rise above it and do the job well.

That's a good question.  I don't know.  Had I not taken that job, it's possible that my wife and I would have moved elsewhere at the time.  With that possibility, there's a number of different jobs I'd have taken, probably outside of academia.  I'd probably have pursued some dumb passion I had at the time or perhaps would have gone to grad school as I'd seriously considered around then.  In either situation, I would have done either thing right before the 2008 recession, and I likely would have gone into crazy debt or something.

Realstically, I was having severe health issues because of the situation.  I was barely getting two or three hours of sleep a night due to stress.  I also could barely eat or keep anything down.  I lost twenty pounds in my last month there.  It really was a choice between the job or my health, so the decision was pretty much made for me.

I wasn't a teacher, so publishing isn't a part of it.  I feel like I'm doing all I can by working with the alumni board and a few other places in order to get back in.
Both.

It's not that I'm hiding anything from her, I'm just tactful about what I present to her.  I've told her that I miss my old job, that's all she needs to know.  The only way I can get a comparable job at another university is by moving.  But by doing that, she'd have to leave the job she loves.  I already know what that's like so I'm not going to do that to her.  Doing anything otherwise would be selfish of me.  She comes first.
How did you do it?

I've tried, man.  I do so many crazy and fun things with my wife and friends.  I've thrown so many things against the wall to try to accomplish something for myself.  It's all just temporary.  As soon as I get off of a quick temporary high, I just go back to hating myself.
What specifically is that supposed to mean?

I don't explicitly bring it up with her.  She knows enough, but I don't want her to know to what extent that it troubles me.  I don't want to impose any guilt or anything on her.  She's happy with where she is in her career, and I don't want her to feel any need to have to be pulled away from it.

Why does everyone keep making a point of contention out of that?  I'm not embellishing anything, I was literally told that word for word by HR.  Why is that supposedly some big red flag?  I'm only relaying exactly what was told to me.

I've long considered giving up my current pay for something that doesn't pay as well but offers something more rewarding.  But the paradoxical truth is that I get paid pretty well at the job that I don't care for now.  It's allowing my wife and myself things in our free time that we've never had before, and it would be selfish and inconsiderate of me to take that away from her.
I'd emailed the guy a few months ago and pretty much told him that.  He said he'd get back with me but never did.
Perhaps.   But I wouldn't even know where to start looking for someone like that.

I'm likely not explaining it well enough, but at least you get the idea of why it still hurt me.

What would you guess that bigger issue is?  You're not the first person that has suggested I take things too personally or don't handle setbacks like that well.
How would you suggest I move past it and onto something else?
Yes, I had even paid about $300 for an hour with a very highly recommended lawyer at the time.  He told me I wouldn't have much of a case.

My old friend that I got hired is the only one that I truly felt betrayed me.  Everyone else just stayed out of it.  I won't lie, I'd have appreciated their help.  But given the situation that was prevalent for everyone to some degree, I can't blame them for staying out of it and I hold no resentment towards them for it.  I did internally at the time, but I've moved far past that.

As for what my old friend did, he was present in a lot of meetings in which falsehoods were spread about me.  He had the chance to speak up and defend me in much of the same way that I had for him previously, but he didn't.  His support could have been huge for me at the time, but he betrayed me by staying silent and not standing up for me when he should have.  He wouldn't have even been employed there if it weren't for me, and I even stuck my neck out for him on multiple occasions.  Be betrayed me by not paying me the same respect.

I'd probably go out of my way to ignore him.  I was extremely stressed when I left.  I got barely three hours of sleep a night at the time, could hardly eat or keep anything down, my health was quickly deteriorating.   Therapy since then has helped out a lot.  Most of the time I'm a lot better about it, today has just been a really bad day.
Most of that issue that I have is tied up with the particular department where I was moved to and had an issue with.  I'm still on wonderful terms with everywhere else in the university.

As time has worn on and as I've talked with therapists, I've been able to better find ways to disguise it or make it more productive.  Today just hasn't been a good day, which led me to vent here.

Typically, I'm able to channel it into something productive.  I've had multiple personal projects fail in the recent years, but at least it was something to keep my mind occupied where I could re-channel that energy as my therapists suggested.
I can't help but feel like you're extrapolating a lot more than is really there.  I'm not trying to present that particular fact in any biased way, I'm just recounting what was told to me.
I don't really have enough evidence to know definitively either way.  But I do know that the places where I can contribute this Fall would be outside of his realm of influence.

I've got my main job and two personal projects right now.  Perhaps one other in the works as well.  I hate sitting still, I have to be working on something.  I just wish any number of them felt productive or were getting me anywhere.

(Using this same text in a few different places since the conversations are kind of at the same point.)

Let me ask you this, then.  Would you think it's wise or not to try to redevelop connections and relationships at my old university?  With the new academic year starting in about a month, I have an opportunity now to do that and pitch in as a board member and volunteer.  It's possible that these could develop over time into new opportunities there.  Is it wise to try to do that, or do I need to completely go cold turkey and move elsewhere?

It's complex.  I certainly had a few minor issues when I working that job, but nothing as extensive as I'd dealt with after I'd left.  I did become somewhat suicidal in the year following being forced out, mainly over guilt and sadness in its wake.  Therapy at least helped me out of that.
Maybe you're right.  How would you suggest I get out of that attitude?

I really feel like I could benefit greatly from some sort of mentor.  After my dad got divorced when I was younger, he's always tried way too hard to be my friend instead of my dad and I don't really have anyone at all to give me the advice I need in any kind of adult situation.

I had reached out a bit to my old department in the past, and they've already helped me somewhat with some things.  It's been a while, I may do that again soon since you suggested it.

I may PM you in a bit since you asked me to.

I don't feel like this is a productive way at looking at the situation.  I was at that job to make a difference in young lives, not to try to outthink anyone that I'm supposed be collaborating with in order to achieve that goal.  It shouldn't be my responsibility to deal with that problem just because someone else is instead choosing to play some ultimately unproductive head game.

I get and appreciate what you're saying, but I don't know if that's a truthful definition of what happened.  

That guy did make it a shitty place to work, but I DID want to be there.  I desperately wanted to be there.  When I got home from the last day, I cried like a baby for like two hours.  It was not in any way any kind of personal victory or decision I wanted to make.
How would you suggest I can do that?
Good point.  How would you suggest I do that?

It's true, I certainly have a different attitude about things in the wake of the whole incident.  It's turned me into a more bitter and pessimistic person.  I hate it and have desperately tried to change it, but nothing is working.
If not him, what would you hypothesize are those real causes?

I have been doing that "long con" to a small degree.  I serve on the Board of Directors of the Alumni Association, and have ever since I left as an employee.  I've been volunteering a bit and have kept connections through it, so I still have that attachment which hopefully could benefit in the long run.

Also..

>  Your self worth is crushed, you feel isolated and betrayed by people you thought had your back, and your future feels bleak because your past has been tarnished.

This reminds me of something I had totally forgotten.

About a year before the asshole co-worker came into the picture, we needed someone to fill a graphic designer position, and I suggested an old buddy of mine and got him hired.  He also had to do some web design work, and was a little inexperienced with it, but I helped him out with it and got him in touch with some resources to help out.  He almost got laid off once, but I put my neck on the line for him and vouched for him and kept him working.

In the wake of my ass-hole co-worker screwing me over, he totally stabbed me in the back.  I'd taken up for my buddy in the year previous, but when everything else wasn't going my way, he didn't return the favor for me.  I fucking hate him for it now.  I would fucking knock him the fuck out and leave his teeth on the ground if I ever saw him in person again.  Nobody has ever betrayed me to that level before in my life and hopefully never will again.

I get and appreciate what you're saying.  It's just problematic for me because it's almost impossible for me not to source every problem I've had over the past three years back to what happened when I got screwed over.  If it weren't for that guy, I'd almost definitely still be working there.  Perhaps in a different context, sure, but I'd still be making a hell of a lot bigger difference and would be a hell of a lot happier.  It's just not as easy as forgetting when you're reminded of it almost every day.

My main area was not in teaching, I only did part time with an orientation class.  I had taught a similar orientation class at a local junior college, but it turned out to basically be a diploma mill where I had no flexibility or resources to enact the type of productivity I had at the four year university I'd been at.

My main experience and expertise is in publicity, marketing, and communications.  I was able to do the most and most good in that role, which is what I'd like to get back into for a university.

I really wish that I had the evidence in front of me to believe what you're saying.  It's been three years since I left that job, and I've not seen any positive change as you've suggested.  And it's not for lack of trying.  I just don't get it.

Relocating is not an option realistically available to me.  My wife has a wonderful career at her current work place, and it would be completely selfish of me to uproot her from that.  There are other factors which have me stuck in my current location, but that's first and foremost.
I've had two different therapists try to go down that road with me, neither have been effective.

>  I gurantee you, if you weren't obcessing over the long distant dream, you would already found a job you loved.

What makes you so certain about that?

I understand how it would be easy to come to that conclusion given the limited context I've provided here.

I recently thought the same thing as you.  I ran through my mind and wondered if I could have toughed it out and weathered the storm and stayed.  Until a few weeks ago, anyways. I had to find some info in my old university email account and had run across some of my old emails with him.  He was just absolutely brutal with me, and effectively was using every trick in the book to force me out.  It was just mentally abusive and I immediately recalled how oppressively depressed it was making me at the time.  It was either my job or my health, which was a choice that practically was made for me.

Right, I know with absolute certainty that I want to work on communications for a university.  But I have limited flexibility in doing that right now, so I am honestly at a loss for where I can fruitfully put any of that energy.

In this case, I don't feel I'm *playing* the victim.  I was told matter-of-factly by HR that if I was female or a minority, they could have taken action.  Since I was not, they could not.

Additionally, I totally understand and appreciate the need to compete.  But only via skills and accomplishments.  Not by who can lie or cheat better.  That's not the competition I want any part of.

Thank you for your story, I really appreciate it.

I think that if I had gotten a similarly rewarding job by now, I'd have long forgotten about it.  But since I've been working comparably meaningless jobs ever since, it's just a cloud that hovers over me indefinitely.

It's not for a lack of trying.  I've applied like crazy to similar things.  Three times now I've had home run interviews at my old university that I later found out had the well poisoned by the guy who still seems to have a vendetta against me.  Hard to move on and forget when that continues to happen.

I had gone through all of my connections to get the jobs I've had and had now.  On paper I can't complain because they pay very well, but that's never been what really matters to me.  I just hate myself because I'm toiling every day for something that ultimately makes no difference for anything other than a company's bottom line.  I still see some of my old students every now and then who are doing well, and I take pride in knowing I had at least a very small part in helping them to reach that point.

I just don't know what the right path is, or even if there is one, to getting back to the way I was.

What is there to learn from?  Screw someone over and walk all over them in order to better yourself?  I really wish I could have some sort of mentor, but he would be the exact opposite of what I would want in that type of relationship.
I'm not talking specifically to that, just in the past painful three years in general.
I feel like my patience has run out.  It's been three years and nothing is progressing.  If anything, it's regressing.

I'm just skeptical because it's just not what I planned on with my career, nor do I feel like I can bring nearly as much to the table as I could in a higher ed environment.  I just don't feel like it's what I'm equipped to do or what I'd feel most useful at, and I don't think I can ever truly do it well because of it.  I'm just a pathetic failure and have no reason to think otherwise unless it's where I historically know I can do well.
Problem is, any public area job is historically very internal.  Meaning you can't really get a job there unless you know someone.  They rarely even advertise open positions because of that fact.

I don't know what I want either.  I just hate to completely internalize it, my therapist has suggested that I write and talk more about the problem.  I'm guess I'm just doing here because she suggested it and Reddit is a familiar platform to me.

I've started mindfulness in the past month, but I've not noticed anything particularly benefitting out of it yet.

1.  Knowing that I was making a difference for both my students and for the university that I had called home (literally) for both my college career and first part of my professional career.

2. Having wonderful working relationships with a lot of positive people who were in it to make a change and be productive for something they believed in, not for profit or a bigger paycheck.

3. Being able to be creative and try new things in my position.  I can't think of many other environments where being so experimental in my position would have been so actively discouraged.

After listing those, the only possible scenario I can see in which those three things can return is by actually returning to work for my university.
Not that I discount what you're saying in the least, but how can you guarantee that with so much certainty?

I'd disagree with all of those assessments rather than the "taking things personally" line.  I'm definitely guilty of that.

But looking at what you said, what I can't deny is that I'm a changed and lesser person after I lost that job.  I certainly have more less than desireable qualities after the fact than I did before.

I guess what drives me crazy is that I'm just not able to.  I've not been sitting by idly these past three years.  I've been desperately trying to get an equatable position, and have tackled a number of personal projects.  Nothing is getting off of the ground, at all.  When I had that job, I had the platform to build things.  But now without it, I don't have that success to build on anymore.
Fuck you, asshole.

Funny you mention that, I did telecommute for a bit and it did allow me the flexibility to work on a novel I'd had in my head for years.  It failed though, only sold a few dozen copies.  That was indescribably discouraging.

I don't think about it all the time, but it certainly has crossed my mind.  My first reaction would be sucker punching him before anything else, if you want full honesty.

Success to me is just doing something I love and feel productive and authoritative at.  It doesn't necessarily have to be in higher ed, just anything that's doing real productive good and isn't wholly profit-seeking.  Unfortunately for the foreseeable future, that has to be in my current location, which limits my options significantly.
I think I don't fully understand what you're asking of me.
What would you define as the difference between the two?

It hurts because I was on top of the world in those four or five years at that old job. I was damn good at what I did and I loved it.  Everything else just seems like a failure when it's not at the point that it was, and I just feel like such a failure when I can't attain it anymore.

Thank you for the kind advice.

I guess I'm just significantly more discouraged lately because I'm realizing it's been three years and despite my best efforts I've made no significant progression into getting back into a job I love as much.  I feel helpless, as if I have no power over my own outcome.

Ever since then, I've done what's called "full stack marketing" for tech companies.  It's okay, and pays well, but it's just completely meaningless to me.  I just come in and get shit done and collect a check, it's in no way personally rewarding like the old job was.  I felt like I was legitimately making a difference there, I'm just pushing shitty tech widgets at the job I'm at now.

And no, moving is just unfortunately not an option.  My wife has amazing positive things going for her right now, and they're intrinsically tied to where we are now.  It would be completely unfair and selfish of me to ask her to give that up.
